newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico police dislodge, hospitalize hunger strikers.
newsitem.headline: Mexico police dislodge, hospitalize hunger strikers.

text.p: Hundreds of Mexican riot police on Sunday broke up a hunger strike that has gripped the nation's attention, and two protesters, near death after three months of fasting, were forced into a hospital.

Just hours after the two street sweepers, who have consumed little but water and glucose for 96 days, had declared they would take their fast "to the death", riot police launched a pre-dawn raid on their makeshift camp.
The protest, on behalf of 300 street sweepers laid off by the local authority in the southeastern state of Tabasco, had cast a spotlight on miserable working conditions and joblessness in Mexico.
It was also a major embarassment for President Ernesto Zedillo's government. On Saturday, government-mediated talks to reinstate the street sweepers in Tabasco broke down.

The government said the hunger strikers and their colleagues pelted the authorities with sticks and pipes as police swept in early on Sunday. Even the ambulance that carried the weakest protestors to hospital was damaged, it said.
But representatives of the strikers said the police started the aggression, beating the street sweepers with batons and almost cracking one protester's skull.

"Between 3 and 4:30 a.m, some 300 riot police armed with sticks dislodged 21 workers and took three to hospital," said Rafael Alvarez of the Miguel Agustin Pro Human Rights Centre, a legal adviser to the street sweepers.
In a statement, the Mexico City government said it had sought to end the hunger strike "for humanitarian reasons" because the lives of the hunger strikers were in danger.

But opposition politicians complained that officials at the Xoco hospital had refused to give any detailed information on the three interned hunger strikers, beyond saying that two were in intensive care.
The third was in less risk because he had been on hunger strike for less time, the authorities said.

The fate of the two longest-standing hunger strikers had deeply moved Mexicans, and doctors said they were likely to suffer permanent physical or mental damage. As recently as Saturday night, they had resisted efforts by their colleagues to hospitalize them.

Even though several other street sweepers resumed their hunger strike outside the National Human Rights Commission on Sunday, the removal of the two weakest members was bound to lessen the street sweepers bargaining clout.
